tagline: An old plank-road corridor links communities where potters still work.
intro: Pottery Road follows NC 705 through Seagrove, Whynot and Robbins toward Eagle Springs. The highway is marked as a North Carolina Scenic Byway for the concentration of potters in and near Seagrove. They make both functional vessels and artistic pottery.

Parts of NC 705 follow the old Plank Road, whose construction began in 1849. The wooden road carried horses, wagons and stagecoaches; railroad competition reduced its toll income, and much of it was abandoned by 1862. Around 1920, motorists traveling toward Pinehurst, Southern Pines and Florida created a new pottery market, encouraging a shift from utilitarian vessels to decorative souvenirs. Interstate construction later diverted passing traffic, contributing to another pottery decline from the 1950s through the 1970s. Renewed interest followed, and local potters established a museum and festival in 1982.

From Seagrove, head southeast through Whynot, then into Moore County near Dover and Westmoore. Jugtown Pottery lies near NC 705, east of Whynot. Continue through Robbins, then turn southeast with the highway beyond its junction with NC 24/27. The drive ends on NC 211 at Elberta, near Eagle Springs.

moments.title: Whynot
moments.text: German and English settlers established the community in the eighteenth century, alongside other settlements in the area. Whynot began as two words, “Why Not.” Residents debating a name settled on it after a man proposed naming the town Why Not and going home. The community is one mile southeast of Seagrove on NC 705. Pottery making here began in the eighteenth century, and several pottery shops continue that work. Whynot also housed the Why Not Academy and Business Institute, a combined public and private school that operated from 1893 to 1916.

moments.title: Jugtown
moments.text: An orange pie dish led Jacques and Juliana Busbee to Moore County in 1917. They found a tradition of utilitarian pottery, then opened a Greenwich Village store in 1918 to sell it. The Raleigh artists founded Jugtown Pottery in 1921. J. H. Owen, Charlie Teague and Ben Owen were among the potters they worked with. Vernon and Pam Owens opened the Jugtown Museum in 1988, after Vernon bought the pottery in 1983. The 1999 National Register listing includes a log sales room, a log turning room and two sheltered kilns, all built about 1921.

moments.title: Robbins
moments.text: Mechanics Hill, Elise, Hemp, Robbins: this town’s names trace its changing industries and patrons. Alexander Kennedy established a rifle factory near Bear Creek after arriving in 1795. Railroad development brought a new town plan and the name Elise, honoring railroad owner John B. Lennig’s daughter. The name changed to Hemp in 1935 to avoid confusion with another town. In 1943 the legislature made it Robbins, honoring textile manufacturer Karl Robbins, who had bought the local mill in 1930. Robbins also supported a water-treatment plant and wastewater-disposal system, completed in 1937, as well as a baseball park.
